tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: On the motion "This house believes that remote work should replace office work", the team that must defend the motion is called the:
options: Adjudication panel, which decides how the motion should be read
Opposition, which carries the burden of proving the motion
Chair's team, which keeps the order and the time of the speeches
Proposition, which carries the burden of proving the motion

questions.question_text: The primary burden of the Opposition in a policy debate is to:
options: Repeat the Proposition's case with a different set of examples
Prove the motion true by using the facts supplied by the Proposition
Show that the proposed change is worse than the status quo or a counter-model
Avoid making any argument of its own until the final speech

questions.question_text: A first speaker for the Proposition defines the motion as "only office workers in a single tiny firm", making the case impossible to oppose. This tactic is called:
options: Weighing, a comparison of the two sides' arguments
Squirreling, an unfair narrowing of the motion
Signposting, an outline of the structure of the speech
Rebuttal, a response to the other side's arguments

questions.question_text: A good definition of the motion should be:
options: Vague, so as to allow the Proposition to change its case later
Complex, so as to display the vocabulary of the first speaker
Fair, reasonable and in line with the ordinary meaning of the words
Narrow, so as to leave the Opposition with little to argue

questions.question_text: A Point of Information in British Parliamentary debate is best described as:
options: A brief question or remark offered to the speaker who has the floor
A ruling from the adjudicator on the winner of the round
A prize for the speaker who offers the most interjections
A summary of the debate given by the chair at the end

questions.question_text: When a Point of Information is offered, the speaker holding the floor may:
options: Ignore it completely, even if the chair asks for it to be taken
Accept or politely decline it, and should take at least one or two in a speech
Accept it only if it comes from a member of the same team
Refuse it only by shouting to the offering member to sit down

questions.question_text: In British Parliamentary format, POIs cannot be offered during:
options: The middle five minutes of a speech, called open time
The first and last minute of a speech, called protected time
The reply speeches given by the whip of each side
The time taken by the chair to announce the next speaker

questions.question_text: The most effective way to rebut an opponent's argument is to:
options: Describe the opponent's motives in order to discredit the claim
Tell the audience that the argument has already been refuted
Restate your own case in a louder voice
State the point fairly, show why it is flawed and give evidence

questions.question_text: A speaker says, "My opponent wants to abolish all offices and destroy the economy", though the opponent only proposed hybrid work. This is a:
options: Burden of proof
Point of Information
Straw man fallacy
Weighing of arguments

questions.question_text: An argument that is built correctly in a debate contains a:
options: Claim, supporting reasoning, evidence and a link back to the motion
Claim and a joke to keep the audience awake and interested
Quotation and the name of the person who first said it
Statistic and the number of the page in the book

questions.question_text: In the PEEL structure for a debate paragraph, the letters stand for:
options: Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link
Premise, Emphasis, Emotion, Logic
Plan, Example, Edit, Learn
Position, Effect, Evaluation, Language

questions.question_text: Quoting "a famous professor says remote work is good" without saying who or where is weak because it:
options: Lacks a verifiable source and so has little credibility
Is likely to be answered by the opponents in the next speech
Is based on the opinion of the experts on the subject
Contains too many facts for the audience to remember

questions.question_text: A speaker says "A 2022 survey of 2,000 employees found that 62% felt more productive at home." This is persuasive mainly because it is:
options: Short, emotional and dramatic
Specific, sourced and quantitative
Spoken in a loud and confident voice
Related to a very popular topic among the youth

questions.question_text: Anecdotal evidence, such as "my cousin loves working from home", is generally:
options: Strong support because it is personal and honest
Better than a survey because it is real
Weak support for a general claim about all workers
Equal to expert opinion on the subject

questions.question_text: The observation that two trends occur together does not prove that one causes the other. In debating, this warns against confusing:
options: Principle with practice
Definition with description
Correlation with causation
Rebuttal with refutation

questions.question_text: During a clash, the closing speaker explains why her side's arguments matter more than the other side's. This technique is called:
options: Squirrelling or narrowing
Interjecting or offering a POI
Weighing or comparison
Signposting or outlining

questions.question_text: "I shall make three points. First, cost; second, productivity; third, well-being." This opening is an example of:
options: Squirreling
Signposting
Rebuttal
Weighing

questions.question_text: Under the principle of "matter, manner and method", "manner" refers to:
options: The result of the debate as announced by the adjudicators
The structure of the speech and the organisation of the case
The content of the arguments and the evidence given in them
The delivery of the speech, such as voice, gestures and fluency

questions.question_text: "Matter" in a debating speech refers to:
options: The style of speaking, including the voice and the gestures
The order in which the points are arranged in the speech
The time that is taken for each part of the speech
The content, including the arguments, analysis and evidence

questions.question_text: "Method" in a debating speech refers to:
options: The structure and organisation of the speech and the team's case
The way in which the audience receives the speech
The tone and fluency of the speaker during delivery
The facts and figures that are quoted in the speech

questions.question_text: Introducing a completely new argument in the reply or final speech is generally frowned upon because:
options: It makes the speech too long to be heard fully
It reduces the number of the points made earlier
The other side has no chance to respond to it
It is not allowed by the timekeepers of the debate

questions.question_text: A speaker finishes a seven-minute speech in only three minutes. The adjudicators are likely to think that:
options: The case has not been fully developed or explained
The speaker was too nervous to sit down properly
The speech was admirably efficient and to the point
The chair had asked the speaker to speak briefly

questions.question_text: The motion "This house regrets the rise of social media" asks the debaters to argue whether:
options: The speakers prefer one social media site to another
A new law should be passed to regulate the social media
Social media is a fact that has occurred in recent years
The world would be better had the development not occurred

questions.question_text: A motion beginning "This house would ban..." is a:
options: Comparative motion between two alternatives
Fact motion about whether something has happened
Value motion about whether something is good or bad
Policy motion that calls for an action to be taken

questions.question_text: A motion beginning "This house prefers a world with..." calls for:
options: A narration of the history of the thing in question
A comparison between two worlds with and without the thing
A proposal for a law to bring that world about
A definition of the thing by the first speaker alone

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: In a debate on whether a city should introduce a congestion tax, an argument that the tax is too complicated to collect is an argument about:
options: Credibility
Humour
Feasibility
Principle

questions.question_text: An argument that the tax is unfair because it burdens the poor more than the rich is an argument about:
options: Delivery or manner
Feasibility or enforcement
Principle or fairness
Timing or kairos

questions.question_text: In a debate, "impact" refers to:
options: How long the argument took to present
How many speakers made the same argument
How loudly the speaker delivered the argument
Why an argument matters and what follows if it is true

questions.question_text: The "status quo" in a policy debate refers to:
options: The change proposed by the first speaker of the Proposition
The final verdict announced by the adjudicators
The opening of the debate by the chair
The existing state of affairs without the proposed change

questions.question_text: A "counter-model" is:
options: An alternative policy proposed by the Opposition instead of the Proposition's model
A question asked of the Proposition as a Point of Information
The same policy as the Proposition's, but explained more briefly
The adjudicator's feedback on the performance of the Opposition

questions.question_text: Which of the following correctly reflects the ideal tone of a debating speech?
options: Hesitant and apologetic, to avoid offending the other side
Confident and respectful, attacking ideas and not persons
Aggressive and personal, to unsettle the other side
Humorous throughout, to keep the audience entertained

questions.question_text: The best response to a personal remark from an opponent is to:
options: Walk away from the podium until the remark is withdrawn
Reply with a remark about the opponent's background
Ask the chair to disqualify the opponent at once
Stay calm and bring the discussion back to the argument

questions.question_text: A speaker begins "Madam Chair, honourable adjudicators and fellow debaters". This is an example of:
options: A casual greeting unsuited to the occasion
A Point of Information offered to the chair
A formal address suited to the debate
A rebuttal to the previous speaker's argument

questions.question_text: The role of a timekeeper is to:
options: Speak on behalf of the chair when the chair is absent
Signal the minutes and warn the speaker about the time left
Decide the winner on the basis of the time taken by each speaker
Offer POIs to speakers who have crossed the limit

questions.question_text: The role of the chair in a debate is to:
options: Prepare the case of the team that is short of speakers
Judge the debate and announce the winner of the round
Keep the score of the arguments made by each team
Preside, call the speakers in order and maintain decorum

questions.question_text: A team fails to turn up and the other team is declared the winner without a contest. This is called a:
options: Rebuttal
Tie-break
Reply
Walkover

questions.question_text: In a British Parliamentary debate, there are how many teams in the round?
options: Six
Three
Four
Two

questions.question_text: The "extension" in the Closing Government's speech is expected to be:
options: A summary of the whole debate without any new material
A new and distinct argument that the Opening Government did not make
A rebuttal of the Closing Opposition's extension alone
A repetition of the Opening Government's strongest argument

questions.question_text: Lincoln–Douglas debate is usually:
options: Three speakers per side, focused on policy and facts
One speaker per side, focused on values and principles
Four teams of two, focused on extensions and whips
A panel discussion without any fixed sides at all

questions.question_text: The Asian Parliamentary format uses:
options: Two teams of three speakers each
Four teams of two speakers each
Two teams of two speakers each
Three teams of three speakers each

questions.question_text: The key difference between a debate and a group discussion is that in a group discussion:
options: Participants work collaboratively without fixed sides
Participants are strictly divided into two opposing teams
Participants must speak in a fixed order set by the chair
Participants are scored for each speech separately by judges

questions.question_text: In a group discussion, a strong participant is one who:
options: Speaks first and longest to dominate the discussion
Contradicts every point made by the other participants
Listens, builds on others' points and speaks briefly and clearly
Addresses the evaluator and ignores the other members

questions.question_text: The person who concludes a group discussion should:
options: Repeat his own opening statement at greater length
Criticise the participants who spoke very little
Introduce a new point to leave the evaluators surprised
Summarise the points covered and the consensus reached

questions.question_text: A flowsheet (flow) in debating is used for:
options: Recording the time taken by each speaker in the round
Planning the seating of the teams in the debating hall
Tracking the arguments and responses made during the round
Collecting the votes of the audience on the motion

questions.question_text: Research before a debate should ideally cover:
options: Only the issues that the opponent is likely to ignore
Both sides of the issue from credible sources
Only the opinions available on social media
Only your own side, to avoid confusion

questions.question_text: A source is most credible when it is:
options: Anonymous, widely shared and entertaining
Old, popular and quoted by many people
Sponsored by a party that gains from the claim
Authoritative, recent and free from obvious bias

questions.question_text: When quoting a source in a speech, a debater should:
options: Name the source and keep the quotation brief and accurate
Read a long passage so that the entire context is given
Attribute it to a famous person to give it weight
Quote from memory, even if unsure of the words

questions.question_text: You suspect that your opponent's statistic is wrong. The appropriate way to respond is to:
options: Question its source or interpretation politely
Ignore it and hope the judges miss it
Quote a larger statistic without any source
Call it a lie in front of the audience

questions.question_text: You cannot answer a POI that has been put to you. The best approach is to:
options: Ask the chair to dismiss the member who offered the POI
Invent a fact to appear well-informed
Ignore it and carry on without looking at the member
Admit it honestly and promise to deal with it later in the speech

questions.question_text: A speaker repeats "We will fight for fairness, we will fight for justice, we will fight for equality". The device used is:
options: Anaphora, or rhetorical repetition
Weighing, or a comparison of arguments
Squirreling, or an unfair definition
Ad hominem, or a personal attack

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: "Do we want a future in which our children cannot breathe clean air?" is an example of a:
options: Definition of the motion
Point of Information
Rhetorical question
Burden of proof

questions.question_text: Presenting ideas in groups of three, such as "faster, cheaper, better", takes advantage of:
options: The rule of five, which makes ideas easier to prove
The rule of one, which makes ideas easier to count
The rule of three, which makes ideas easier to remember
The rule of two, which makes ideas easier to refute

questions.question_text: The best opening to attract the audience's attention is:
options: An apology for being unprepared for the debate
A relevant, surprising fact or a question linked to the motion
A joke that has no link with the subject of the debate
A long list of thanks to everyone present in the hall

questions.question_text: A good conclusion to a debating speech:
options: Introduces two fresh arguments to stay ahead of the opponents
Restates the stance and summarises the main arguments briefly
Ends in silence so that the audience can think
Apologises to the audience for the time taken

questions.question_text: When judges give feedback after a round, a debater should:
options: Leave the room before the feedback is given
Listen with respect and use it to improve
Argue with the adjudicators to change the result
Treat it as unimportant if the team has lost

questions.question_text: A debater who sticks rigidly to a written script is likely to:
options: Sound less natural and find it hard to respond to the other side
Sound more confident and be better able to respond
Be rewarded for the careful preparation shown
Score higher on method because the script is detailed

questions.question_text: Eye contact in debating helps the speaker to:
options: Engage the audience and appear sincere and confident
Reduce the need to prepare the speech in advance
Conceal the fact that notes are being used
Distract the opponents while they take notes

questions.question_text: The persuasive appeal that depends on the speaker's credibility is:
options: Logos
Kairos
Ethos
Pathos

questions.question_text: "As a doctor with 25 years of practice, I can tell you that this treatment works." The appeal used is mainly:
options: Ethos
Pathos
Logos
Kairos

questions.question_text: "Imagine a mother waiting alone in the dark for her child." The appeal used is mainly:
options: Pathos
Kairos
Ethos
Logos

questions.question_text: Which statement is a verifiable fact rather than an opinion?
options: India's population is a blessing for its economy.
India's population is too large for its resources.
India's population crossed 1.4 billion in 2023.
India's population will cause trouble for the world.

questions.question_text: An opinion becomes a persuasive argument when it is:
options: Expressed by a senior member of the team
Repeated several times with greater volume
Supported by reasons and evidence
Printed in large letters on the speaker's notes

questions.question_text: If one team makes a point and the other side never responds to it, it is generally treated by the judges as:
options: Void, as no one has supported it in the round
Standing unchallenged, and so carrying weight
Disallowed, as it was not responded to by the opponents
Withdrawn by the team that made it

questions.question_text: Which of the following is NOT a skill that debating helps to develop?
options: Accepting claims without examining the evidence
Research and the organisation of ideas
Public speaking with confidence
Critical thinking about arguments

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a good way to prepare for an impromptu debate in the 15 minutes given?
options: List the stakeholders, arguments on both sides and examples quickly
Wait to hear the other team and then think of a case
Choose one example and speak on it for the full time
Write the full speech word for word and memorise it

questions.question_text: "Stakeholders" in the analysis of a motion are:
options: Only the members of the audience in the debating hall
The people or groups who are affected by the issue
Only the adjudicators who will decide the round
Only the shareholders of the companies involved

questions.question_text: The Proposition's "model" is:
options: The Opposition's response to the policy of the Proposition
The chair's summary of the policy of the Proposition
The adjudicator's ruling about the policy of the Proposition
The specific policy it proposes to implement the motion

questions.question_text: "This house believes..." motions generally ask debaters to:
options: Propose a detailed law or a policy
Narrate a story from history
Define each word of the motion at length
Defend or oppose a belief or a stance

questions.question_text: In a closing speech, the speaker should avoid:
options: Comparing the two sides' arguments on their importance
Responding to the main clashes in the round
Summarising the strongest points of the team
Repeating earlier points without new analysis or comparison

questions.question_text: Judges are asked to decide which team debated better, not which side they personally agree with. This means that the judges should:
options: Vote for the team that spoke the loudest
Vote for the team that had more speakers
Vote for the side they personally support
Set aside their own opinions on the motion

questions.question_text: A "clash" in a debate is:
options: A quarrel between the speakers on the stage
A direct point of disagreement between the two sides
A change of the motion by the chair
A tie declared between the two teams

questions.question_text: "Role fulfilment" in judging means whether the speaker:
options: Spoke for the maximum duration of the time given
Did what his position in the team required at that point
Wore the proper dress for the competition
Took the maximum number of POIs in the round

questions.question_text: A speaker who has taken no POI and offered none in a British Parliamentary debate:
options: May be marked down for not engaging with the other side
Is treated as having conceded the debate to the other side
Is disqualified from the round by the chair
Is rewarded for staying focused on his own speech

questions.question_text: A speaker offers a POI every ten seconds to a rival. This behaviour is:
options: Required by the rules of the debate
Disruptive and likely to be penalised
Admirable as it shows constant engagement
Rewarded as a sign of confidence

questions.question_text: A debater uses humour that mocks an opponent's accent. The adjudicators are likely to:
options: Treat it as a strong rebuttal
Reward it for being witty and light
Ignore it since humour is not judged
Penalise this for being disrespectful

tests.title: Unit 7: Fundamentals of Debating – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: The best use of an analogy in a debate is to:
options: Explain a complex idea by comparing it with a familiar one
Confuse the opponents about the point being made
Avoid giving any evidence for the claim made
Prove the point by itself, without any further reasoning

questions.question_text: An analogy is weak when:
options: The two cases differ in the features relevant to the argument
The two cases share several relevant features in common
The comparison is supported with evidence from experts
The comparison is explained clearly to the audience

questions.question_text: "Either we ban the product entirely, or we accept thousands of deaths." This argument is a:
options: False dilemma
Straw man
Circular argument
Slippery slope

questions.question_text: "If we allow even one exception, soon all the rules will be abandoned." This argument is a:
options: False dilemma
Post hoc
Slippery slope
Red herring

questions.question_text: A speaker replies to a criticism of his policy by saying "And what about the policies of your party in 1990?" This is:
options: A Point of Information to the critic
A definition of the motion
A fair rebuttal that directly answers the criticism
Tu quoque, deflecting the criticism with a charge against the critic

questions.question_text: Which of the following best explains why the Opposition might prefer a status quo defence?
options: The Opposition is not permitted to propose an alternative
The change proposed may carry risks that outweigh its benefits
The Proposition has the burden of explaining the status quo
The status quo is always better than any change

questions.question_text: In a debate, an unsupported claim like "Everyone knows that remote work is bad" is weak because:
options: It uses too many facts for the audience to follow
It is likely to be answered by the opposition at once
It offers an assertion without reasons or evidence
It contains too many sources for the judges to check

questions.question_text: "Weighing" arguments requires the speaker to:
options: Compare the loudness of the speakers of the opposing teams
Measure the length of the speeches made by each team
Explain why one's impacts are larger, likelier or more important than the opponent's
Count the number of arguments made by each side and pick the larger

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a principled argument for a motion about free speech?
options: Free speech costs less to administer than censorship does
Free speech will increase the number of tourists visiting the country
Free speech is popular among the young people of the country
People have a basic right to express their opinions without censorship

questions.question_text: Which of the following is an example of a pragmatic argument for the same motion?
options: Open debate helps governments to detect and correct their own errors
People have a natural right to say what they think
Silence is contrary to the spirit of democracy
A free voice is a part of human dignity

questions.question_text: Which skill does a debater use when listening carefully and noting the opposing team's claims for rebuttal?
options: Passive hearing
Active listening and flowing
Reading from the script
Memorising the speech

questions.question_text: A debater should avoid using jargon with a general audience because:
options: The judges do not know the meaning of the terms
The jargon is always incorrect for the subject
The use of terms is banned by the rules of debating
The audience may not follow the terms and the point may be lost

questions.question_text: To make an argument memorable, a speaker can use:
options: A series of unrelated statistics
A string of difficult words
A concrete example or a short story to illustrate the point
A long list of abstract definitions

questions.question_text: "Equity" in judging a debate means that the judges should:
options: Favour the team with less experience in debating
Give every team a fair hearing, whatever their background
Favour the team that belongs to their own college
Favour the team that spoke at the greatest length

questions.question_text: When a debate has ended in a tie on the points, the adjudicators can usually break the tie by:
options: Asking the audience to vote by raising their hands
Tossing a coin to select one of the two teams
Looking at the overall quality of matter, manner and method
Asking the chair to nominate the better-dressed team

questions.question_text: A debate speech that ignores the strongest argument of the other side is usually considered:
options: Brilliant, as it saves time for new arguments
Out of order, as it breaks the rules of speaking
Incomplete, as it fails to engage with the main clash
Dishonest, as it contains false facts

questions.question_text: The best way to respond to a clever but irrelevant point by an opponent is to:
options: Spend the whole speech answering it in great detail
Pretend that it was never made by the opponent
Ask the chair to strike it off from the record
Briefly show why it is irrelevant and return to the main issue

questions.question_text: Which behaviour shows good sportsmanship after a debate?
options: Leaving the venue without speaking to anyone
Complaining about the result to the audience
Criticising the judges on social media
Shaking hands and thanking the opponents and the judges

questions.question_text: The adjudicators' decision in a debate is usually:
options: Based on the performance in the round, not on prior reputation
Based on the number of the supporters of each team
Based on the opinion of the audience in the hall
Based on the prior reputation of the teams in the circuit

questions.question_text: Debating on a motion that you personally disagree with helps to:
options: Change your view to that of the opponent permanently
Prove that the opponent's view is correct
Avoid taking any stance on a matter in future
Understand the opposing viewpoints and sharpen your reasoning

questions.question_text: A speaker who uses a short pause before an important point is making use of:
options: A request to the chair to offer a POI
A loss of the thread of the speech
Emphasis through silence
A mistake in the timing of the speech

questions.question_text: A debater repeatedly says "um", "like" and "you know". The best way to reduce these fillers is to:
options: Pause silently and think before starting the next sentence
Add more fillers so that the habit looks deliberate
Speak faster so that the fillers are not noticed
Avoid making eye contact with the audience

questions.question_text: The most important duty of a debater towards the truth is to:
options: Hide the facts that are against his side
Present facts accurately and not distort the evidence
Invent examples to win the round
Use only the facts that favour the opponents

questions.question_text: A team gives the same argument under three different headings in its case. The judges would probably say that the team:
options: Has followed the correct method of case construction
Has fewer distinct arguments than it appears to have
Has presented three distinct and strong arguments
Has reached the maximum score for matter

questions.question_text: The most important quality of a successful debater is:
options: A long speech that fills the time given
Clear thinking communicated with respect for the others
A loud voice that dominates the room
The habit of interrupting the opposing speakers
